item.title: Quick Take — Veridical Data Science (audiobook)
item.description: This book is about practicing data science in a way that is genuinely trustworthy. The central argument is that getting useful, reliable results from data requires more than applying algorithms — it requires critical thinking, domain knowledge, and a principled framework for evaluating whether your results hold up. The authors call this veridical, meaning truthful, data science.
item.itunes:author: Bin Yu and Rebecca Barter

item.title: Ch. 1 — An Introduction to Veridical Data Science
item.description: To practice veridical data science is to practice "truthful" data science. The goal is to answer real-world questions by collecting and critically evaluating relevant empirical, data-driven evidence, using human judgment calls in the context of domain knowledge. If that evidence is deemed sufficiently trustworthy, it gets communicated to domain stakeholders, where it can play a role in real-world decision making and in updating what we know about the domain.
item.itunes:author: Bin Yu and Rebecca Barter

item.title: Ch. 2 — The Data Science Life Cycle
item.description: Every data science project progresses through some combination of six stages. The book calls these stages together the data science life cycle, or DSLC. The six stages, in order, are: first, domain problem formulation and data collection; second, data cleaning, preprocessing, and exploratory data analysis; third, exploration of intrinsic data structures through dimensionality reduction and clustering; fourth, predictive and inferential analysis; fifth, evaluation of results; and sixth, communication of results. Almost every project will pass through stages one, two, five, and six. Stages three and four are optional — whether you need them depends entirely on the question you are asking.
item.itunes:author: Bin Yu and Rebecca Barter

item.title: Ch. 3 — Setting Up Your Data Science Project
item.description: In this chapter, we step back from the analytical substance of data science and look at the scaffolding around it — how you structure your files, write and document your code, and organize your workflow so that your results are reproducible and your project remains intelligible to collaborators and to your future self. The ideas here draw directly on the data science life cycle and the predictability, computability, and stability framework introduced earlier in the book.
item.itunes:author: Bin Yu and Rebecca Barter

item.title: Ch. 4 — Data Preparation
item.description: Every data science project begins with a question and a dataset, but rarely does the dataset arrive ready to use. The chapter opens with a concrete image: you are a journalist, or perhaps a researcher, trying to understand organ donation rates around the world. Before you can answer any question about trends or rankings, you need to confront the data itself — its inconsistencies, its missing entries, its inconvenient formatting. That confrontation is the subject of this chapter.
